about.title: Richmond Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Falls rarely make the news the way collisions on I-80 or Richmond Parkway do, but for the roughly 110,000 people who live in Richmond, a bad fall inside a grocery store, a rental complex, or a parking structure can be every bit as disruptive. The core of a California premises liability claim is notice: you generally have to show the owner or manager knew about the hazard, or reasonably should have known, and failed to repair it or warn you. That is why what you do in the first few days matters so much. Photographs of the spill, the loose tile, or the missing handrail, names of anyone who saw it, and a prompt written request that the business keep its surveillance footage can make the difference between a claim that holds up and one that fades. LawProactive is not a law firm. We are a free service that connects Richmond residents with an independent attorney in our network, and those attorneys work on contingency, so there is no fee unless your case recovers money.

whyChoose.title: Why Richmond Residents Turn to LawProactive After a Fall

items.title: Attorneys who understand the notice requirement
items.desc: Proving the owner knew or should have known about the hazard is the hinge of a California premises case. The independent attorneys we connect you with build claims around inspection logs, prior complaints, and how long the condition existed.

items.title: Fast action to preserve video and evidence
items.desc: Store and apartment cameras often overwrite footage within days. Getting an attorney involved early means a preservation demand can go out before the recording of your fall disappears.

items.title: Clarity on deadlines and shared fault
items.desc: Most California premises claims carry a two-year filing deadline, but claims against a city, county, or other public entity are much shorter. California's pure comparative fault rule also means you can still recover even if you were partly responsible, with the award reduced by your share.

items.question: I fell on a sidewalk or in a park owned by the City of Richmond. Is the process different?
items.answer: Yes, and the timing is tighter. Claims against a California public entity such as the City of Richmond or Contra Costa County generally require a written government claim within six months of the injury, well before the two-year deadline that applies to private property owners. Missing that window can end the claim entirely, so it is worth speaking with an attorney quickly. Documenting the exact location and condition of the defect is also especially important with public property.

items.question: The store manager said the spill had only been there a minute. Do I still have a case?
items.answer: Possibly. Under California law, the question is whether the owner knew or reasonably should have known about the hazard and failed to address it, which often turns on how often the area was inspected and whether the store can actually prove it. Surveillance video, sweep logs, and employee statements frequently tell a different story than what is said at the scene. An attorney can request those records before they are lost.

items.question: I was looking at my phone when I slipped. Does that mean I get nothing?
items.answer: No. California follows pure comparative fault, meaning your recovery is reduced by whatever percentage of blame is assigned to you, but it is not eliminated. If a jury found you 30 percent responsible, for example, you could still recover 70 percent of your damages. The attorneys in our network evaluate these situations honestly and can tell you how shared fault might affect your claim.
